abstract: Lipid droplets, once viewed primarily as lipid storage organelles, are increasingly recognized as key regulators of cellular homeostasis, which is particularly critical during seed imbibition and germination. Here, we investigated the role of the selective autophagy receptor AtNBR1 in lipid droplet-associated processes during Arabidopsis seed germination. AtNBR1 and ATG8 proteins were specifically and transiently recruited to lipid droplets during germination. Confocal imaging revealed their predominant colocalization in condensate-like puncta adjacent to lipid droplets and, less frequently, in autophagosome-like structures surrounding them. Mobile AtNBR1-positive lipid droplet remnants were also observed within the vacuole, particularly under treatments that simultaneously stimulate autophagy and limit vacuolar degradation. Besides, AtNBR1 degradation was modestly reduced in an atg2 mutant, which is consistent with a minor NBR1-associated macrolipophagy-like pathway. Moreover, AtNBR1 does not appear to mediate a major route of lipid droplet degradation, as loss of AtNBR1 did not significantly affect bulk lipid turnover or the degradation of ubiquitinated and non-ubiquitinated oleosins, the major seed lipid droplet proteins, arguing against oleosins being primary AtNBR1 cargoes. Instead, our data support a broader role for AtNBR1 in seed proteostasis. AtNBR1 interactome comprises multiple protein quality control components, including the post-proteasomal exopeptidase TPPII. AtNBR1 also colocalized with CDC48A and PUX10, components of the lipid droplet-associated degradation pathway, and PUX10 contributed to AtNBR1 turnover. Importantly, loss of AtNBR1 compromised seed longevity in an accelerated aging assay. Together, our findings suggest a role for AtNBR1 in protein quality control at lipid droplets and support its positive contribution to seed longevity.
